Deep dive · minerals and miningDraft for review

Africa's minerals

Africa mines 77% of the world's cobalt, 80% of its platinum and 63% of its manganese ore. Of the 22 minerals on this page it produces half or more of the world's output of seven: rhodium, tantalum, platinum, cobalt, manganese ore, chromium ore, diamonds. Most of it comes from a handful of countries. In 2024 DR Congo alone mined 75% of the world's cobalt, South Africa 70% of its platinum and 54% of its chromium ore, Guinea 35% of its bauxite and Mozambique 25% of its titanium minerals.

Where it goes is another map. Of the USD 163.8 bn of ores, concentrates and first metals that the rest of the world reported buying from African countries in 2024, China took 45% and Europe 24%. China bought 91% of the bauxite, 88% of the cobalt and 75% of the chromium. Gold is the blind spot. The United Arab Emirates, which reported buying USD 37.0 bn of African gold in 2023, had not reported 2024 to UN Comtrade, so the USD 52.6 bn of gold counted here is a floor.

Rare earths are the exception. Africa mined about 1.1% of the world's rare earths in 2025, from Madagascar and Nigeria, against China's 270,000 tonnes. But the USGS puts 890,000 tonnes of rare-earth oxide in Tanzania's reserves and 860,000 in South Africa's, and the projects to mine them are contested. A Chinese company, Shenghe, bought Tanzania's Ngualla in 2025; the United States, the European Union and Japan back projects in South Africa, Malawi, Angola, Namibia and Madagascar. Of the 16 projects in this page's register, two are producing and two are being built.

Data fetched 13 Oct 2026 · production from the BGS (2000–2024) and the USGS (2025) · 695 mines and plants and 1,183 deposits from the USGS · trade from UN Comtrade (2024) · a draft, not linked from the site

Where the mines are

521 mines and 174 processing plants of these minerals that the USGS located across Africa for 2018, with their operators and owners; 1,183 known deposits; and 1,048 exploration projects. Pick a layer and a mineral: the countries take that mineral's share of world production and only its sites stay on the map. Hover a country or a site for the detail.

Mines and plants are the USGS's compilation of Africa's mineral industry (2021), from its Minerals Yearbook country chapters for 2018: a site's status is as of 2018 ("assumed active" means the yearbook listed it without a note), its capacity is the yearbook's, and owners are as reported then; some have changed hands since. Only sites of the page's minerals are drawn; the cement, steel, salt, coal and other industrial-mineral sites are in the data file, and oil and gas are left out. Deposits are where the USGS records ore, not a list of working mines: from its major mineral deposits of Africa and the Middle East (Open-File Report 2005-1294) and its critical-mineral deposits of the world (Professional Paper 1802, 2017); a deposit in both is drawn once. Exploration projects are from the USGS World Minerals Exploration Database, each last confirmed active between 2004 and 2018. Shares of world production as in the chart above. Borders and lakes from Natural Earth.

Who owned the mines

The 460 mines of the page's minerals that the USGS compilation lists as working or being built in 2018 (not those on care and maintenance or closed), by where their owners were based. Each mine counts once, split by its owners' equity stakes; an owner counts for the home country of its ultimate parent, and a government or company of the mine's own country counts as "host". This is a count of mines, not of their output or value: a small gold mine weighs as much as Kamoto. 92% of the equity could be classified; the rest is the grey track. Hover a row for the largest owners.

Across all of them, companies and miners of the mine's own country held 30% of the equity and its government 17%; European companies 21%, Chinese 6.1% and North American 6.7%. In the copper and cobalt mines, European companies, Glencore first, held 31% and 41%, Chinese companies 22% and 12%. Australian companies held 38% of the titanium mines, governments 89% of the phosphate mines, and local and artisanal miners most of the tin and tantalum mines.

Twenty-five years of output

Africa's share of world mine production each year from 2000 to 2024, from the BGS. Hover a panel for the year, the share and the largest African producer.

What is left in the ground

Africa's share of the world's known reserves (orange) beside its share of 2025 mine output (blue), for 17 minerals, from the USGS. Reserves are what can be mined at a profit with today's knowledge and prices, as companies and governments report them, so they move with prices and with exploration.

The USGS names only the larger reserve holders and leaves some countries' reserves unreported ("NA"), so Africa's share is a floor. Platinum-group reserves are for all six metals; output is platinum's. Iron is by iron content, bauxite and phosphate by marketable rock, titanium as TiO2 in ilmenite.

Where it goes

What the rest of the world reported importing from African countries in 2024, by destination: ores and concentrates, and the first metals made near the mine (cobalt hydroxide, copper cathodes, ferrochrome, gold bars, rough diamonds). Hover a row for the values and the largest exporters.

ChinaEuropeGulf statesIndiaUnited StatesJapan and South KoreaOther African countriesEverywhere else

UN Comtrade, imports reported by partner countries ("mirror" data, which is more complete than many African customs' own), in US dollars at the importer's border. Trade through a hub shows the hub: gold refined in Switzerland or the Emirates, diamonds sorted in Belgium or Dubai, cobalt and copper that cross Zambia or South Africa on their way. Europe here is the EU, the United Kingdom, Switzerland and Norway; "everywhere else" is led by Indonesia for chromium, Thailand and Malaysia for copper, Canada and Australia for gold, and Pakistan and Türkiye for phosphate. Importers reported 387 tonnes of gold from South Africa in 2024, 4 times the 90 tonnes mined there (BGS): the rest is gold refined in or traded through South Africa, which customs records count as South African. The United Arab Emirates is missing: it had not reported its 2024 imports when this was fetched. In 2023 it reported buying USD 37.0 bn of gold from African countries, most from Guinea, Mali and Ghana, and USD 6.9 bn of diamonds; the bars leave that year out, so the gold and diamond rows understate the Gulf.

Rare earths

The seventeen metals in the magnets of wind turbines, electric motors and guided missiles. China mines most of the world's and refines nearly all of it. Africa mined 1.1% of world output in 2025 (USGS: Madagascar 2,700 tonnes of rare-earth oxide, estimated from China's imports, and Nigeria 1,500, against China's 270,000), but holds known reserves of 890,000 tonnes in Tanzania and 860,000 in South Africa, and some of the most advanced projects outside China. 16 of them are in the register below, compiled on 13 Oct 2026 from ministries', regulators' and the owners' own filings: two producing, two being built, eight at feasibility, two earlier and two stalled.

StageProducingBeing builtFeasibilityExplorationStalledother USGS rare-earth deposits
  • Madagascar's USGS figure does not come from mine reports. It is "estimated based on reported import data for China". Source
  • USGS cut its estimate of Nigeria's 2024 output from 13,000 t REO (January 2025 edition, estimated from Chinese import data) to 1,500 t (February 2026 edition). Madagascar's 2024 figure fell from 2,000 t to 1,400 t. Source · Also
  • Tanzania (890,000 t REO) and South Africa (860,000 t) are the only African countries with quantified rare-earth reserves in the USGS table. World reserves exceed 75 million t, and USGS records no mine output from either country in 2024 or 2025. Source
  • In June 2025 the EU named 13 'Strategic Projects' outside the bloc under its Critical Raw Materials Act. The only two rare-earth projects among them are African: Mkango's Songwe Hill in Malawi and Frontier Rare Earths' Zandkopsdrift in South Africa. Source
  • The US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) said in August 2026 that it had committed $62.8 million to rare-earth projects in Malawi, Angola, Madagascar and South Africa, none yet in production. Most of it is the $50 million it would put into TechMet's option on a stake in Phalaborwa, which Rainbow Rare Earths' own filings describe as not yet exercised. Source · Also
  • Malawi banned exports of raw, unprocessed minerals from 21 October 2025 by presidential executive order. Rare earth elements are named in the order's list, but minerals processed in Malawi are exempt. Source
  • In June 2023 Namibia's Cabinet banned exports of unprocessed critical minerals, and rare-earth minerals are named in the ban. Small quantities can still be exported at the mines minister's discretion, with Cabinet endorsement. Source
  • The African Union's Green Minerals Strategy, adopted by the AU Executive Council in February 2025, says rare earths are mined in Angola, Burundi, Madagascar and South Africa. It lists projects in development in Malawi, South Africa, Tanzania, Madagascar, Morocco and Mozambique. Source
  • In April 2025 China tightened export controls on several rare earths, including terbium and dysprosium, and kept those controls after suspending a wider October 2025 extension. Source

Export rules that touch rare earths (6)
  • Namibia, 2023-06. Cabinet banned exports of unprocessed critical minerals: crushed lithium ore, cobalt, manganese, graphite and rare-earth minerals. Smaller quantities may be exported at the mines minister's discretion, subject to Cabinet endorsement. The decision was announced by Deputy ICT Minister Emma Theofelus at a Cabinet briefing. No gazette notice was found. Source
  • Malawi, 2025-10. A presidential executive order banned exports of raw, unprocessed minerals from 21 October 2025. It names uranium, rare earth elements, niobium, graphite, tantalum and others, and exempts minerals processed, refined or value-added in Malawi. Lindian Resources says Kangankunde is unaffected because it will export a concentrate. Source
  • Malawi, 2026-02. In his February 2026 State of the Nation address, President Mutharika suspended all new mining licences and ordered an audit of existing permits. The October 2025 raw-export ban stays in place. Source
  • Tanzania, 2017. The 2017 overhaul of the Mining Act gives the government a non-dilutable free-carried interest of at least 16% and restricts exports of raw resources for beneficiation abroad. This applies to all minerals. At Ngualla, Tanzania holds a 16% free-carried interest in Mamba Minerals, the licence holder. Source
  • Uganda, 2015-02. A ban on exporting unprocessed minerals, imposed by President Museveni in February 2015, 'still stands', Energy Minister Ruth Nankabirwa said in October 2022. Rare earths are not named. Source
  • Nigeria, 2025-05. No gazetted ban was found. Nigeria makes local processing a condition of new licences, and Solid Minerals Minister Dele Alake said in May 2025 that 'The days of exporting raw minerals from pit to port are over.' Rare earths are not named. Source
Looked at and left out (36)
  • Glenover (Limpopo). Owned by Afrimat (JSE) since 2021, not Fertoz. Only a techno-economic assessment / concept study has been done for rare earths (SAMREC 19.47 Mt @ 1.52% TREO+Y2O3; 647 ha mining right; phosphate stockpiles processed). Afrimat says it is still optimising the flowsheet. No PFS or DFS. Metallurgical test work was done in South Africa, China, Germany and the USA. Sources: https://www.afrimat.co.za/future-materials-metals/ and https://www.afrimat.co.za/press-releases/the-glenover-rare-earth-project/
  • Mineral sands monazite (Richards Bay Minerals, Tronox Namakwa Sands, MRC Tormin). Heavy mineral sands operations, known monazite/thorium hosts. No rare earth project or study announced.
  • Tundulu / Nathace Hill (Malawi). Exploration only, no JORC resource; AuKing Mining agreed in Apr 2026 to buy 100% (DY6 Metals named as earlier holder in press). Not an Mkango asset.
  • Eturra (Malawi/Tanzania). No rare-earth project of this name found in any search.
  • Machinga (Malawi). Early exploration (prospecting licences, AuKing deal up to A$4m); seen in search snippets only, not fetched.
  • Salambidwe (Malawi). Undrilled exploration ground (AuKing via Green Exploration); search snippets only.
  • Chambe Basin, Mulanje (Malawi). Ionic-clay exploration; licence expired Feb 2020 and outcome of re-application unknown; search snippets only.
  • Other Tanzanian REE projects. No other Tanzanian rare-earth project at feasibility stage or beyond found; a May 2026 overview says none beyond Ngualla.
  • Mauze (Malawi). No standalone project found; the 2022 Songwe NI 43-101 report only notes that Songwe Hill abuts Mauze Hill.
  • Chilwa-area mineral sands (Malawi). No rare-earth project at feasibility stage or beyond surfaced in searches.
  • Eureka (Namibia; ReeXploration Inc., formerly E-Tech Resources, TSX-V). Monazite discovery at trenching/exploration stage, no resource-based study found; 2026 work is a uranium drill programme
  • Kameelburg (Namibia; Aldoro Resources, ASX:ARN, AU). Large carbonatite resource (about 520 Mt per Ecofin, May 2026) but no published scoping study or PFS found; Ecofin only mentions an ongoing feasibility assessment
  • Eisenberg (Namibia; Broadmind Mining, Namibian private). Inferred resource only; no granted mining licence or feasibility study found (licence application within EPL 6688 reported); 2022 target of 2026 production not evidenced
  • Ondoto (Namibia; Ondoto Rare Earth, private). Private bastnaesite project; no public feasibility study found
  • Coola (Angola; Pensana). Exploration carbonatite 30 km from Longonjo; Sep 2026 farm-out to ASX-listed Tyranna Resources (US$2.6m over 3 years, Pensana diluting to 20%)
  • Sukulu / Osukuru (Uganda; Guangzhou Dongsong Energy Group, CN). Phosphate fertiliser and steel complex; rare earths only a planned by-product, no REE study or production found
  • Busumbu / other Tororo carbonatites (Uganda). No current REE project, study or licence found
  • Second Ionic Rare Earths project in Africa. None found; Ionic's other assets are outside Africa (Brazil, UK recycling)
  • Bekisopa (Akora Resources, Madagascar). Iron ore project, not REE (per brief); not researched.
  • Kwale mineral sands (Base Titanium, Kenya). Titanium/zircon sands; no REE or monazite product found in this pass; not researched further.
  • Ruri Hills (Kenya). Carbonatite REE prospect at early exploration; no feasibility-stage work found; not researched.
  • Other Burundi or Gabon REE prospects. None at feasibility stage or beyond found in this pass.
  • Nigeria monazite concentrate output (artisanal and small-scale). Real and counted by USGS (about 1,500 t REO a year), but no mine, operator or plant is named in any source. See nigeria_output.
  • Monte Muambe (NeoTerra Group, ex-Altona Rare Earths), Tete, Mozambique. Pre-feasibility not done. Contractor for the USTDA-funded PFS was picked on 20 Aug 2026, with the study due to start in Sep 2026. Has a 25-year mining licence and a JORC resource of 13.6 Mt at 2.42% TREO.
  • Kenmare Moma mineral sands, Mozambique. Monazite only as a minor part of the mixed ZrTi by-product concentrate (Q2 2026 report). No separate REE product and no REO tonnage disclosed.
  • Dingsheng Minerals, Chibuto, Mozambique. Chinese heavy mineral sands (titanium) operation, reported stalled in 2026. No monazite or REE product found (search only).
  • Egyptian Black Sand Co., Burullus plant, Egypt. Sands plant inaugurated Oct 2022 (NMA holds 15%). Monazite was named as planned output, but no evidence it is separated or sold. The USGS 2024 Egypt chapter has no rare-earth row.
  • Eramet Grande Cote (GCO), Senegal. Eramet markets only zircon and titanium products from GCO; no monazite or REE product. No REE row in the USGS 2024 Senegal chapter.
  • Sierra Rutile / Sembehun, Sierra Leone. Rutile, ilmenite and zircon only; no monazite product found (search only). No REE row in the USGS 2024 Sierra Leone chapter.
  • Nkombwa Hill, Zambia. Exploration only; old JORC resource and no study found. Marula Mining gave up its interest in Dec 2024 (search only).
  • Bou Naga, Mauritania. Mined for yttrium and thorium in 1967-68 only; no current project found (search only).
  • Lamlaga and Twihinate prospects (ONHYM with Managem), Morocco. Exploration prospects only (search only).
  • Gcwihaba (Tsodilo Resources), Botswana. Conceptual exploration target only, with drilling planned for 2026 (search only).
  • Chishanya and Kapfrugwa, Zimbabwe. Old exploration (Prospect Resources 2021, Rainbow 2019); no current project found (search only).
  • Cameroon, DR Congo, Cote d'Ivoire, Ethiopia, Ghana, Guinea, Mali, Rwanda. No REE project at feasibility or beyond found. The USGS 2024 country chapters for these, and for Egypt, Mauritania, Mozambique, Senegal, Sierra Leone and Zambia, contain no rare-earth production row.
  • Hasetins rare earth and critical metal processing plant (Nigeria). A processing plant under construction whose feedstock and products are not disclosed; the state governor named platinum, uranium and chromium. Not shown as a rare-earth project on the evidence found.

  • Phalaborwa DFC: Miningmx (5 Oct 2026) says DFC 'has already committed $50m towards construction funding'. Rainbow's Dec 2023 RNS and Mar 2026 interims call it a US$50m equity option via TechMet, not exercised. DFC's Apr 2024 public summary says DFC 'proposes to invest up to $50 million in equity' (https://www.dfc.gov/sites/default/files/media/documents/9000116135.pdf). Treat it as an option unless DFC or Rainbow confirm.
  • Phalaborwa: did Bosveld complete the notarial lease and the transfer of the stacks to an SPV (long-stop 31 Dec 2025)? Rainbow's option to buy Bosveld's 15% for 38.9m new shares runs to 30 Jun 2027.

Offtaker Neo (Toronto HQ) has plants in Canada, Estonia, China, Germany, Thailand and the UK. Traxys and two US family offices joined the Mar 2026 GBP 11.1m (c. US$14.6m) raise (https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/rainbow-rare-earths-limited-npv--rbw/subscription-raises-11-1m-from-investors/9499206). COR-23 dates are unconfirmed. The reserve excludes a pending Section 102 extension. The NI 43-101 report date is not stated. The site's text says 665,000 t @ 14.5%, but its table gives 605,000 t @ 14.4%.
  • Steenkampskraal: the IDC funding amount and its terms (loan or equity) are undisclosed.
  • Zandkopsdrift: reserve tonnage and grade from the 2025 updated PFS were not found. Older figures such as 41.12 Mt @ 1.92% TREO (c. 2015) appeared only in search snippets and were not verified. Stakes of Frontier, IDC, KOMIR and the BEE holders are unknown. No coordinates were found in a fetched source.
  • Zandkopsdrift: Frontier says multiple EU funding pathways are being evaluated (News24, Feb 2026). Watch for EU, EIB or Carester-linked finance.
  • Malawi export rules: Presidential Executive Order No. 2 of 2025 bans raw-mineral exports; the MMRA letter of 28 Oct 2025 says Kangankunde is exempt because monazite is concentrated in Malawi before export. Draft Beneficiation and Value Addition Regulations and amendments to the Mines and Minerals Act 2023 were under consultation until 10 Oct 2026. https://wcsecure.weblink.com.au/clients/lindianresources/headline.aspx?headlineid=61346521 ; Mining Minister quoted 24 Sep 2026 saying no company may export raw minerals: https://www.nyasatimes.com/lindian-resources-moves-to-upgrade-licence-as-malawi-tightens-mineral-export-rules/

Outcome not found. https://allafrica.com/stories/202608040027.html ; https://justice.gov.mw/node/566

  • Songwe export: the Mar 2026 DFS lists Malawi government approval to sell the MREC as a risk; the MREC is to go to Mkango's planned Pulawy plant in Poland for separation. https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/mkango-resources--mka/feasibility-study-songwe-pfs-results-pu-awy/9481471

  • Tanzania rules: law gives the state not less than 16% non-dilutable free-carried shares in a mining company and a right to acquire up to 50%.   • Teesside (UK): Peak secured a site for a rare earth refinery, then dropped it in favour of a standalone concentrate project and sold it on 9 Jul 2025 for GBP 3.5m. https://announcements.asx.com.au/asxpdf/20250811/pdf/06mrcb48sjb3qs.pdf
  • Ngualla takeover price: shareholders were paid A$0.443 per share on 30 Sep 2025, above the A$0.359 minimum in the May 2025 deal (total A$157.99m at signing). Press reports of an A$195m final value were not verified.
  • Ngualla output: older press cites 37,200 t/y concentrate; the Aug 2025 scheme booklet gives 16.2 kt/y. The booklet figure is used.
  • Ngualla coordinates are from Wikipedia (Mount Ngualla), not a technical report; treat as approximate.
  • Wigu Hill: former owner Montero Mining agreed to settle its dispute with Tanzania over the project for US$27m in three instalments (date not visible on page). https://www.northernminer.com/news/montero-mining-settles-with-tanzania-for-us27m/1003875175/ No Vital Metals update on the licence after 2023 was found.
  • Songwe MDA: Mining Development Agreement signed 26 Jul 2024 (announced 29 Jul 2024) with a 5% royalty on gross revenue and a 10% non-diluting equity interest for the Malawi Government. https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/mkango-resources--mka/mkango-signs-mda-with-malawi-government-for-songwe/8334631
  • Ngualla licence changes: the SML area was expanded from 18 to 51 km2 and the initial term extended to 30 years (announced 26 Apr 2024). https://announcements.asx.com.au/asxpdf/20250811/pdf/06mrcb48sjb3qs.pdf
  • Kangankunde licence detail: Lindian names it Mining Licence MML0290/22 (medium-scale) and says approval was given during FY2026 to enlarge the area from about 900 to 2,500 ha. https://wcsecure.weblink.com.au/clients/lindianresources/headline.aspx?headlineid=61345643
  • Namibia: Cabinet in June 2023 banned export of unprocessed critical minerals 'such as' crushed lithium ore, cobalt, manganese, graphite and rare earth minerals, with ministerial exemptions for small volumes (https://www.mining-technology.com/news/namibia-ban-unprocessed-minerals-export). Apr 2026 said 38.2% of Sable Min for US$150m; the June 2026 update says about 4% of Pensana and of Sable Min; Aug 2026 says State of Qatar backers widened scope to downstream and a NASDAQ listing, with US$150m still outstanding (https://pensana.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Update-on-Cascade-Financing-6-August-2026.pdf).   • Ampasindava: the exploitation permit number, grant date, term and area are not in the 12 Oct 2026 RNS. Licence PR6698 appears only in secondary coverage, which was not fetched. Some outlets give the DFC amount as $4.48m, but the RNS says $4.84m. Harena signed the Cahier des Charges Minières (CCM) on 11 Aug 2026 (RNS https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/harena-resources-plc--hree/mining-terms-and-conditions-ccm-signed/9714357). Reuters via Engineering News (https://www.engineeringnews.co.za/article/us-backs-madagascar-rare-earths-project-in-push-to-loosen-chinas-supply-chain-grip-2026-07-28, Jul 2026) named MP Materials, USA Rare Earth and Solvay (EU) as potential refining partners; no offtake is signed.
  • Vara Mada: no news on the investment agreement after Aug 2026. AllAfrica (May 2026) says it must be approved by the High Constitutional Court and Parliament before work starts (https://allafrica.com/stories/202605040006.html). No Madagascar state equity is disclosed; the Dec 2024 MOU reportedly includes a 5% royalty, but this was not fetched. Coordinates were not found.
  • QMM: the monazite resource/reserve was not fetched (Rio Tinto 20-F too large). Monazite volumes since 2019 and buyer names are undisclosed. The Ecologist reports operations were suspended Nov 2025 to 6 Jan 2026, which may explain a lower 2025 figure. Rio Tinto has put its titanium business under strategic review.
  • Gakara: AFP reports a presidential order suspending foreign miners from 14 Jul 2021, which was not fetched. Rainbow still describes government actions as not in line with the mining convention, with no resolution as of Mar 2026. Historical offtake was not researched.
  • Mrima Hill: sources disagree on the Cortec licence date. afaa.ngo gives 2013; Citizen/bilaterals report a 10 Apr 2015 cancellation of 65 licences by CS Najib Balala. Resource figures in news (5.8 Mt Nb / 48.7 Mt REE, or 6.4/53.6 Mt) are unverified and not used. The tender winner and the outcome of the 9 Oct 2026 ruling are unknown.
  • Mrima Hill bidders: RareX and Iluka (AU) filed a joint application with NAMICO in Apr 2025. A US consortium, Mrima Earth Ltd, has also bid, and Chinese state companies reportedly signalled interest (https://miningmx.com/news/battery-minerals/2026-04-07-kenya-opens-bidding-for-prized-rare-earths-deposit). President Ruto said Kenya and the US finalised a preliminary agreement on the site (https://citizen.digital/article/petition-filed-to-stop-proposed-kenya-us-mrima-hill-mining-deal-n385178).
  • Mabounié: GabonReview (Feb 2026) says 'Eramet-Comilog en détient 76%', which contradicts Eramet's Nov 2022 sale of all assets to the state. Unresolved, not used. NEM/Dusk's stake, the state's share and the resource reporting code are unknown. Also involved: Indonesia (Perminas/Danantara) and Gulf (NEM, Abu Dhabi); Eramet (FR) exited in 2022.
  • No Japanese or Russian involvement was found in any of these projects.
  • Nigeria: none of the fetched sources say whether the monazite is a by-product of tin and columbite mining or tailings on the Jos Plateau, or which states produce it. USGS names no area or company. RMRDC sampled monazite in Kano, Taraba, Plateau, Kaduna and Bauchi in 2025.
  • Nigeria buyers: USGS MCS 2025 estimated Nigerian output from Chinese import data, which points to China as the buyer, but no fetched source gives monazite export tonnage by destination. The USGS 2024 chapter records tin, beryllium and tantalum going to China, but no destination for monazite.
  • Nigeria export ban: no gazetted ban on raw-mineral exports found. The Oct 2023 'era of exporting raw materials is over' line from the minister is a policy statement, and the USGS 2024 chapter mentions no restriction. Value addition seems to be enforced through licence conditions (search only).
  • Hasetins: is this an REE separation plant at all? Feedstock, flowsheet, products and the existing 6,000 t operation are all undisclosed. Rare Earth Exchanges (Dec 2025) says no Chinese ownership or partnership has been disclosed. Keep it, flag it, or drop it at merge.
  • Mineral sands rule: Kenmare sells monazite only inside a mixed concentrate (ZrTi). The same yes/no rule should apply across clusters, e.g. Madagascar or South African sands with incidental monazite.
  • Egypt Burullus: EBSC's head was quoted (Oct 2022) as expecting '145k tons of monazite' a year. That is implausible next to 298k t ilmenite and USGS world totals, and is probably a misquote. Treat it as unverified.
  • Kaduna polymetallic discovery with rare earths announced Jul 2026 at an Abuja summit (search snippet only; not fetched).
  • The USGS Tanzania reserve (890,000 t REO) almost matches Ngualla's JORC ore reserve of 887 kt REO in Peak's August 2025 scheme booklet. USGS likely took its figure from it, but USGS does not say so. Where USGS's South Africa figure (860,000 t) comes from is not stated.
  • In MCS 2026, Nigeria's 1,500 t no longer carries the 'estimated from Chinese import data' footnote. USGS says only that the revision is 'based on Government and industry reports'. Which reports, and why the figure dropped from 13,000 t to 1,500 t, is unexplained.
  • Burundi (Gakara), Angola and Malawi have no USGS rows. Any output is inside 'Other' (550 t in 2025), with no breakdown. The AU strategy says rare earths are 'mined' in Angola and South Africa, but USGS shows no output for either.
  • The AU strategy cites Madagascar at 960 t in 2023 (from USGS 2024). USGS 2025 gives 2,100 t for 2023. Madagascar's figures have moved a lot between editions.
  • Of the DFC's $62.8m, the $12.8m split among Malawi, Angola and Madagascar was not in the fetched Reuters text. Search snippets claiming $3.4m for Longonjo, a $4.6m grant for Songwe Hill and a potential EXIM loan of up to $160m for Pensana are unverified.
  • The AFC/Absa Longonjo loan was approved in March 2025, subject to conditions. No financial close was confirmed. A reported US$100m strategic investment in Pensana (December 2025) was not fetched.
  • Namibia: no gazette notice or legal instrument was found for the 2023 ban. It is not checked whether it was later amended, how it treats concentrates (such as Lofdal's), or whether it is enforced.
  • Malawi: the official text of the executive order was not found. Whether a mineral concentrate counts as 'processed' rests on Lindian's own statement; no government ruling was found.
  • Uganda: a January 2025 government post 'President Museveni Restates the Prohibition on The Export of Raw Minerals' (infrastructure.go.ug) returned 404. How the ban applies to Makuutu's mixed carbonate is unknown.
  • Zimbabwe: the December 2022 ban, a circular under the Base Minerals Export Control Act, covers lithium only (miningindex.co.zw). The 'SI 213/2022' designation appears only in search snippets. A reported later extension to all unrefined minerals (Mondaq) was not fetched. It is left out of export_rules because rare earths are not covered.
  • Ghana: the 2023 Green Minerals Policy and the December 2023 raw-lithium stance do not name rare earths in any source found. It is left out of export_rules.
  • EU: a second list of projects outside the EU has not been published. The 9 October 2026 list covered EU applications only, and the next call is due 'towards the end of 2026'.
  • JOGMEC/Lofdal: a Crux Investor report says JOGMEC and Toyota Tsusho completed their earn-in in July 2026. This is unverified; no company filing was fetched.
  • Not found: any US Minerals Security Partnership project list naming African rare-earth projects, any US-Malawi or US-Uganda critical-minerals MoU, or official confirmation of the February 2026 Rubio ministerial with African states.

Country by country

Every African country that mines 1% or more of the world's output of one of these minerals, has three or more deposits on the map or exported more than USD 50 million of them in 2024. The platinum-group metals count once.

How this page was made

Production
The British Geological Survey's World Mineral Statistics, through its open API, for mine production by country from 2000 to 2024. It names every producing country, so Africa's share is a whole share. Where a country reports a total and its parts (gem and industrial diamonds, grades of ore), the total is taken. Contains British Geological Survey materials © UKRI 2026, used with the acknowledgement BGS asks for. For lithium, tantalum and rare earths, whose BGS tables mix ores, concentrates and contained metal country by country, the USGS's 2025 figures are used instead.
Reserves
The USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 (public domain), read from its "World Mine Production and Reserves" tables. The USGS folds smaller producers into "other countries" and leaves some reserves unreported, so Africa's shares from it are floors.
Mines and plants
The USGS Compilation of Geospatial Data (GIS) for the Mineral Industries and Related Infrastructure of Africa (2021): every mine and processing plant in the USGS Minerals Yearbook's African country chapters for 2018, located, with its commodities, capacity, status, operator and equity owners. A site listed once per commodity is drawn once. Oil and gas fields and refineries are left out. Status and owners are as of 2018. Its exploration layer (the USGS World Minerals Exploration Database) is the map's third layer.
Owners
The owners' home countries are this page's classification, not the USGS's: each owner counts for the home country of its ultimate parent in 2018, from the parent's filings and listing; a government or company of the mine's own country counts as "host". The full list is in the review table under the chart, and in minerals_owners.json. A mine's equity is split by the stakes the USGS gives; owners listed without a stake share what is left.
Deposits
Two USGS datasets from its ArcGIS server: Open-File Report 2005-1294 (major mineral deposits of Africa and the Middle East) and Professional Paper 1802 (critical-mineral deposits of the world, 2017). Each point is placed in a country by its coordinates; a deposit listed in both, within about 8 km and with a mineral in common, is drawn once.
Trade
UN Comtrade's public API: imports reported by every other country in 2024 from each African country that mines the mineral (per the BGS and USGS), for the HS headings of its ores and first products (listed in the table). Values are at the importer's border, in US dollars; goods refined or re-exported in a country count as that country's. A country that has not reported a year is missing from it: in 2024 that is the United Arab Emirates, whose last reported year is given beside the chart and never added in. Lithium's heading, 2530.90, also holds other minerals, so its row is approximate. Rare earths are left out: Africa's concentrates ship under headings shared with other ores.
Rare earths
A register kept by hand in minerals_ree.json: each project with its owners and their home countries, its stage, resource, buyers and lenders, and the address each fact was read from: ministries, regulators' filings (ASX, TSX, LSE, JSE), technical reports and development banks' own pages.
Files
minerals.json (production, reserves, trade), minerals_sites.geojson (deposits), minerals_facilities.geojson (mines and plants) and minerals_exploration.geojson. Rebuilt with fetch_minerals.py and build_minerals.py.
